title_en: 2026 standout Titanium Court is springing onto consoles and mobile on October 29
title_fa: 2026 standout Titanium Court is springing onto consoles and mobile on October 29
excerpt_en: One of the best games of the year won't be confined to Steam for much longer.
excerpt_fa: One of the best games of the year won't be confined to Steam for much longer.
content_en:
2026 standout Titanium Court is springing onto consoles and mobile on October 29
One of the best games of the year won't be confined to Steam for much longer.
At this point, more video games are released in a month than most folks can play in a lifetime. More than 21,000 games have been released on Steam alone so far this year. Many of those will not be worth your time, but one I can absolutely recommend is Titanium Court. It's one of the best games of the year and many more people will soon get the chance to play it. The game is coming to Nintendo Switch, Switch 2, PlayStation 5, Android and iOS on October 29.
Titanium Court debuted on Steam back in April. It made waves earlier in the year after winning the Seumas McNally Grand Prize at the Independent Games Festival Awards. Developer AP Thomson (who also won that award in 2025 as part of the team that made Consume Me) has crafted a beguiling run-based game that hasn't been far away from my thoughts for the last six months. It's a roguelite but also a visual novel and at the same time an RPG.
🚨 Titanium Court has escaped from our computers! 🚨
📣 It's marching towards Nintendo Switch 1 and 2, PlayStation 5, iOS, and Android 🎮 📱
Brace yourselves; it arrives on October 29!
— Fellow Traveller (@fellowtraveller.games) 2026-10-14T16:02:05.662Z
A run (which is called a "war" here) is made up of multiple battles, each of which has two phases. The first is essentially a match-three game in which you'll move around tiles representing things like wheat, rivers, forests and enemy castles. Line up three matching tiles, and you'll gain relevant resources or wipe enemy strongholds off the map. At the same time, you're setting up the battlefield for the second stage, in which baddies will attempt to attack your base, which is also a tile on the grid. Before this phase starts, you can use resources to shore up your defenses by recruiting soldiers and other workers.
That's the main thrust of the gameplay, but there's so much more to Titanium Court. The game shackles you from trading too much at stores and it might block you from carrying out what you think is a winning tactic. You can't really break the game's rules as you can in incremental roguelites like CloverPit and Balatro. Figuring out what the restrictions are is part of Titanium Court's charm.
That extends to the meta-game that takes place between runs. Your character is the court's new queen, who is initially clueless as to what's going on. They don't know how they ended up in this bizarre kingdom, where road signs exist alongside dragons as well as faeries that don't believe in the concept of cars. On your quest to get home, you may encounter references to baseball, Jenga and all manner of pop culture touchstones.
Titanium Court is a stylish, clever and wildly offbeat game. It's packed with jokes and surprises so I don't want to give too much more away here. I'm excited to dive into it again, probably on my phone to hopefully dissuade me from doomscrolling.

title_en: Android will use Gemini to warn you about scammy messages
title_fa: Android will use Gemini to warn you about scammy messages
excerpt_en: Google will tell if you a scammer is trying to message you and will protect your banking details from prying eyes while sharing your screen.
excerpt_fa: Google will tell if you a scammer is trying to message you and will protect your banking details from prying eyes while sharing your screen.
content_en:
Android will use Gemini to warn you about scammy messages
Google has announced new scam and privacy protection tools for Android.
Google has announced a bunch of new, expanding and upcoming scam protections for Android users, including an opt-in setting in its Messages app that uses Gemini AI to warn you about deceptive messages. Toggling on the setting will enable Scam Detection, which taps into Google's most advanced Gemini models to evaluate the sender's intent and warn you if the messages could be coming from a bad actor. In Google's example, the sender pretended to show the recipient a photo of them with their dog. Upon being told that they had the wrong number, the sender tried to engage and asked the recipient their name.
The company explained that Android analyzes messages in Private AI Compute, which encrypts them and processes them in a secure space inaccessible to anybody else, even Google. Gemini Nano will also do on-device analysis of links in Messages to make sure they're safe before you tap on them. This will be available on Google Pixel 10+, the Samsung Galaxy S26 series, Galaxy Z Flip and Galaxy Fold 8, among other select devices. In addition, Google has redesigned its scam warnings to give you more context and extra time before tapping on links sent from numbers not in your contacts list. The new opt-in security setting is rolling out in the coming weeks.
After introducing Scam Detection in chat notifications on Pixel devices, Google is expanding its availability to more devices. The feature will warn you about potential scams right inside the message notification, so you don't even have to view it. Google has teamed up with device manufacturers, including Honor, Motorola, OPPO, OnePlus, realme, vivo and Xiaomi, which are expected to enable the feature later this year.
Meanwhile, all devices running Android 15 and newer will get automatic screen-sharing privacy later this month. The feature will hide passwords, banking information and credit card security numbers by default if you're sharing your screen that has Chrome or Android WebView open. In early December, the company is also rolling out call forwarding protection on Pixel and other select devices. The feature will block apps from secretly enabling call forwarding in the background. Android will warn you if a scammer tries to trick you into typing an MMI forwarding code — a short string of figures — to switch on call forwarding on your device.
Google has reported that it teamed up with banks in Brazil to combat bank impersonation, as well. To make sure it's actually a bank calling, Android will perform a verification check on incoming calls. If the caller fails to pass the check, Android will hang up the call and alert you. Google said Android has already blocked over three million fake calls since launching the feature in June. It's not clear if and when it will bring the safety tool stateside, but the company said it will work with more partner banks in the future.

The company explained that Android analyzes messages in Private AI Compute, which encrypts them and processes them in a secure space inaccessible to anybody else, even Google. Gemini Nano will also do on-device analysis of links in Messages to make sure they're safe before you tap on them. This will be available on Google Pixel 10+, the Samsung Galaxy S26 series, Galaxy Z Flip and Galaxy Fold 8, among other select devices. In addition, Google has redesigned its scam warnings to give you more context and extra time before tapping on links sent from numbers not in your contacts list. The new opt-in security setting is rolling out in the coming weeks.
After introducing Scam Detection in chat notifications on Pixel devices, Google is expanding its availability to more devices. The feature will warn you about potential scams right inside the message notification, so you don't even have to view it. Google has teamed up with device manufacturers, including Honor, Motorola, OPPO, OnePlus, realme, vivo and Xiaomi, which are expected to enable the feature later this year.
Meanwhile, all devices running Android 15 and newer will get automatic screen-sharing privacy later this month. The feature will hide passwords, banking information and credit card security numbers by default if you're sharing your screen that has Chrome or Android WebView open. In early December, the company is also rolling out call forwarding protection on Pixel and other select devices. The feature will block apps from secretly enabling call forwarding in the background. Android will warn you if a scammer tries to trick you into typing an MMI forwarding code — a short string of figures — to switch on call forwarding on your device.
Google has reported that it teamed up with banks in Brazil to combat bank impersonation, as well. To make sure it's actually a bank calling, Android will perform a verification check on incoming calls. If the caller fails to pass the check, Android will hang up the call and alert you. Google said Android has already blocked over three million fake calls since launching the feature in June. It's not clear if and when it will bring the safety tool stateside, but the company said it will work with more partner banks in the future.

title_en: Alibaba AI models cleared for use in Apple Intelligence in China just in time for the iPhone Duo launch
title_fa: Alibaba AI models cleared for use in Apple Intelligence in China just in time for the iPhone Duo launch
excerpt_en: Apple's integrated AI system is still yet to be rolled out in mainland China, despite launching nearly two years ago.
excerpt_fa: Apple's integrated AI system is still yet to be rolled out in mainland China, despite launching nearly two years ago.
content_en:
Alibaba AI models cleared for use in Apple Intelligence in China just in time for the iPhone Duo launch
Apple’s integrated AI system is still yet to be rolled out in mainland China, despite launching nearly two years ago.
Apple Intelligence will soon be making its way to supported iPhone models in China, as the country reportedly rubber stamps the use of Alibaba AI models to power the technology.
As reported by the South China Morning Post, which is owned by the Alibaba Group, China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology has given regulatory approval for Tongyi Qianwen, the group of LLMs better known as Qwen, as well as the Tongyi Wanxiang AI-generated image and video tool.
Apple had already received clearance to roll out Apple Intelligence on the Chinese mainland back in July, but the South China Morning Post's report says it has not yet done so. The updated filings include network access permits for the iPhone Duo and 18 Pro, with the former set to launch in China next week with the new and improved Siri AI as one of its flagship software features.
Much of Apple Intelligence's feature set is already available in Hong Kong, but the mainland's complex AI and privacy laws have required Apple to be patient about bringing what is now a core feature to one of its fastest-growing markets. It will seemingly now arrive almost exactly two years after it launched in the US, where Apple has worked with both Google and OpenAI to train its models and hand off complex questions.
Reports that Apple would seek to work with Chinese AI firms for a workaround to bring Apple Intelligence to the country first emerged as far back as early 2025, with Alibaba named at the time. Back in the summer, it was confirmed that Qwen would be central to Apple Intelligence in compatible iPhone, iPad, Mac and Vision Pro models that it sells to its Chinese customers.

title_en: Deezer will soon let you filter out AI-generated music
title_fa: Deezer will soon let you filter out AI-generated music
excerpt_en: Deezer said that the new toggle will be rolled out by the end of the year.
excerpt_fa: Deezer said that the new toggle will be rolled out by the end of the year.
content_en:
Streaming platform Deezer remains steadfast in its intent to help users avoid listening to AI-generated music: The company on Tuesday said it is working on a new toggle that lets users filter out AI-generated music uploaded to its platform. The feature is expected to be available before the end of the year.
Deezer said turning on the toggle will stop you from seeing AI-generated tracks, albums, and related artists in search results.
“We’ve seen clear user demand for the ability to filter out AI-generated music, and we are now giving everyone the option to remove this content completely from their streaming experience on Deezer, and focus only on human creators and creations, if they wish,” Deezer CEO Alexis Lanternier said in a statement.
He added that the explosion of AI music on the platform was one of the catalysts for the toggle-based features. The company cited a survey from last year, which noted that around 45% of Deezer customers wanted a way to remove AI music from their feeds.
Deezer added AI-detection tooling last year and has been reporting on the number of tracks being uploaded to the platform ever since. At that time, AI-generated tracks represented 10% of daily uploads.
In July, the company said that more than 50% of daily uploads to its platform were AI-generated tracks, with an average of 90,000 tracks per day.
Other music streaming services have also created their own policies in relation to AI music. Bandcamp has completely banned AI tracks, while Tidal cut off monetization for people uploading AI music. Spotify has taken a leaner stance, only tagging AI tracks and artists more prominently on its platform.
In August, Variety reported that Apple Music was looking to label AI tracks by the end of the year. Besides platform-based tagging, users are also turning to independent tracking systems to identify AI music.

title_en: LG adds DTS:X and Google Cast to its Sound Suite home theater system
title_fa: LG adds DTS:X and Google Cast to its Sound Suite home theater system
excerpt_en: LG's latest Sound Suite update includes DTS:X, a much-requested feature.
excerpt_fa: LG's latest Sound Suite update includes DTS:X, a much-requested feature.
content_en:
LG adds DTS:X and Google Cast to its Sound Suite home theater system
The company also teased a 'Media Connect Hub' for DTS:X devices that's currently in development.
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
LG is known for its soundbars and surround sound systems as much as it is for its OLED TVs, and one of its more interesting products in that realm is Sound Suite. That premium system lets you pick and choose select speakers à la carte to best fit your space, place them where you want and then use Dolby Atmos FlexConnect tech make them perform well — a nice setup, if you can afford it.
Now, LG is adding some new features to Sound Suite in response to customer feedback. It now supports DTS:X for new surround sound options, along with Google Cast, dual W7 subwoofers and more flexible Wi-Fi configurations. LG also teased a new "Media Connect Hub" for DTS:X devices that's currently in development.
The key new feature is DTS:X support for the H7 soundbar, the centerpiece of LG's Sound Suite. That feature, it said, will give "home theater enthusiasts additional ways to enjoy immersive, multi-dimensional audio from compatible content and source devices." Another big update is Google Cast support on the H7 soundbar so that you can stream content like music and podcasts directly to LG Sound Suite systems.
In keeping with its flexible multi-speaker underpinning, Sound Suite is also expanding compatibility in home networked environments with support for Wi-Fi 6 GHz networks and 5 GHz DFS channels. That, LG said, will give users more stereo and multi-speaker configuration options within the Sound Suite environment. Finally, LG is adding support for dual W7 subwoofer setups, for those who want to max out on low end sound.
As for the Media Connect Hub, LG said it will enable DTS:X "from compatible external source devices and further expand access to DTS:X content." That's quite vague, but it could be a way to connect Blu-ray or 4K Ultra HD disc players to the Sound Suite environment, along with other devices that support DTS:X. That's just a guess, though, and we'll need to wait for more news from LG on the subject. The new software updates are already rolling out in some regions, but timing and availability could be different depending on your location.

title_en: WhatsApp adds a guest option for joining calls without an account
title_fa: WhatsApp adds a guest option for joining calls without an account
excerpt_en: It's also working on calendar integrations for later this year.
excerpt_fa: It's also working on calendar integrations for later this year.
content_en:
WhatsApp adds a guest option for joining calls without an account
It’s also working on calendar integrations for later this year.
WhatsApp is adding more flexibility for talking to people who aren't regular users of its service. The Meta-owned company has announced the addition of a feature dubbed guest calling. With this option, somebody can join a call even if they don't have a WhatsApp account.
The guest calling support mirrors the little-known option to join a FaceTime call without an Apple account or device. Like that feature, there are some restrictions for participating in a WhatsApp call via the guest method. Guests cannot start a call; they can only receive and accept invitations. They'll also have to be approved by the call host before they can join. A guest will not be able to view other users' phone numbers, send messages or add more members to the call. However, they will be able to join either 1:1 or group calls from a browser, and once approved, guests will be able to use core tools such as screen sharing, raising their hand, and reacting with the thumbs up and heart emojis. Guests also won't have any time limits placed on their participation in a call.
The company noted that it plans to further facilitate collaboration with the future rollout of a plugin for calendar integrations. Once launched "later this year," the plugin will allow WhatApp calls can be created from Google or Outlook calendars.
WhatsApp has kept a brisk pace with feature updates this year, many of them aimed at making the service more accessible, secure and appealing for business users. The addition of usernames allowed people to keep their phone numbers private, while more incremental adds from 2026 include encrypted web calls and account signups via iPad. The service may also offer a much-requested option to schedule messages in advance.

title_en: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake plays even better than it looks
title_fa: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake plays even better than it looks
excerpt_en: Link is getting a lot more than just a visual glow up for the new Switch 2 version.
excerpt_fa: Link is getting a lot more than just a visual glow up for the new Switch 2 version.
content_en:
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake plays even better than it looks
Link is getting a lot more than just a visual glow up for the new Switch 2 version.
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is simply one of the best video games ever. Not only did it redefine a beloved franchise after it made the jump from 2D to 3D following A Link to the Past, it sits alone at the top of Metacritic's all-time rankings, a full point higher than other legendary titles like Soulcalibur, GTA IV and Super Mario Galaxy 2. When Nintendo announced that it was remaking the classic title from 1998, the hype was more than understandable. And now that I've had a chance to play a preview of this new version for the Switch 2, I can safely say that it plays even better than it looks.
It's easy to focus a ton on the game's updated visuals. While the original looked great for a 3D title back in the late 90s when most games were still confined to two dimensions, the N64 had its limits, and more than 20 years later, the game is showing its age. But with this remake, Nintendo has completely reshaped Hyrule and given it a loving makeover befitting a new release in 2026.
With its fresh graphical treatment, everything just feels so full of life. Kokiri Forest is lush and overgrown, while the main square in Hyrule Castle Town is bustling with people and pets. Taller buildings and new alleys add a sense of depth and dimension you didn't really get from the original. But I'd argue that things get even better when you focus on smaller details, like the textures on various items. The wise old owl, Kaepora Gaebora, now appears wonderfully fluffy yet still distinguished, while objects like the Deku Shield fit in even better with its surroundings. Instead of looking like a thick piece of cardboard with a swirl on it, you can actually see the bark it's made out of and how it's just as much a piece of the forest as the rest of the village. Meanwhile, Link's nose finally has a more natural shape, instead of looking like it's sharp enough to cut glass.
Things get even better when you go exploring. Inside the Forest Temple, there are rooms with low lying fog that swirls around as you search for items, which enhances the spooky atmosphere. However, my favorite touch is the new effects you see when Link swings his sword. There are brilliant particles that burst out when you make contact with an enemy while the updated animation for his Spin Attack sends out waves of energy, adding even more emphasis to our hero's signature move.
My one small gripe with the remake's updated graphics is that water doesn't look quite right. For example, after going for a swim, it almost looks like Link is covered in high-fructose corn syrup instead of water. When you check out various streams and rivers, they seem to be filled with light blue jello instead of good 'ole H20. But the appearance of water is something that a lot of modern games still have trouble with and it's easy enough to overlook considering how good the rest of the game's visuals are.
As for gameplay, Nintendo smartly decided not to mess too much with the original's formula. You still rely a lot on Z-targeting (locking onto nearby enemies by pressing one of the Z shoulder buttons), which feels kind of quaint nowadays. However, there is now an actual jump button for navigating platforms and obstacles, which makes running around feel a lot more natural. There's also a new sprint button for quickly getting around. That said, if you want to pretend it's 1998 and roll everywhere, you can do that too, and like the rest of the game's movement, running, fighting and traversing the world feels a lot smoother and less clunky than it did back in the day.
Nintendo also added cutscenes with full voice acting, which adds an extra level of gravitas to things like meeting the Great Deku tree for the first time. And just like before, you still have Navi yelling "Hey, Listen!" at you, which even though it might get annoying after a while, I wouldn't have it any other way. The one small downside to this is that when you're just running around town and talking to lower-level NPCs, dialogue is still mostly text-based, which can make Link's limited speaking abilities feel like something is missing sometimes.
Some other new quality of life features includes the Threads of Time system which adds helpful story summaries and tool tips so it's easier to remember what you were doing in the game and pick up where you left off. You also now have full control over camera positioning in case you get stuck in an awkward position, though I found that I didn't need it very often. Swimming has also been improved a ton and the inventory screen has been reworked too, so swapping between tools and weapons is even faster than before. These are just some of the more obvious upgrades; there are a ton of little or more subtle changes like Link actually pushing on things to open doors, full day/night cycles, tweaks to the game's map and landscape and others. Heck, you can even hum or sing into the Switch 2 to play notes on the in-game ocarina if traditional button inputs aren't your thing. And when you hear tunes like the Song of Time again, it hits hard.
There's just so much going on in the Ocarina of Time remake, even for people like me who played it when it first came out almost thirty years ago. The game still feels fresh and exciting while retaining everything that made it the classic it is today. This means that regardless of whether you're a long-time fan or someone new to the franchise, there's a lot to like and I can't wait to explore how deep all of Nintendo's changes go this time around.
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Switch 2 is available for pre-order now for $60, ahead of its official release on November 5.

title_en: Samsung Health's sleep coaching now requires just three days of data
title_fa: Samsung Health's sleep coaching now requires just three days of data
excerpt_en: Galaxy Watch owners can now get Sleep Coaching faster.
excerpt_fa: Galaxy Watch owners can now get Sleep Coaching faster.
content_en:
Samsung Health's sleep coaching now requires just three days of data
It will then build a tailored four- to eight-week program based on your goals and habits.
Samsung Health has offered Sleep Coaching for several years, but using it required a full week of consecutive sleep data in a month. With this new update, the app will let users start Sleep Coaching faster and provide more personalized sleep guidance. The update also brings a few new features for runners.
With the new version, anyone using a Galaxy Watch 4 series or later model (or the Galaxy Fit 3 or Galaxy Ring) can start Sleep Coaching with just three days of sleep data from the past two weeks.
When setting it up, you need to fill out a survey around your sleep regularity and interruptions, along with alcohol and caffeine intake. It will also ask you to rate how satisfied you are with your sleep. Using your survey responses and three days of data, Health will assign you a personalized Sleep Animal symbol and tailor a four- to eight-week coaching program to your goals.
As you progress, the app will adjust its weekly recommendations to your changing sleep patterns, while tracking your daily sleep satisfaction. It will also provide daily habit checklists and sleep tips, like avoiding screens and caffeine before bed or stretching outdoors after waking up—all based on behavioral sleep science.
Users will get more intuitive, detailed analysis reports, with a five-sided Sleep Balance graph showing sleep time, sleep regularity, nighttime wakefulness, sleep satisfaction and an "Energy Score" to highlight areas needing attention. It also provides daily morning insight messages that review your previous night's sleep and offer helpful tips.
Samsung is also boosting its Running Coach app for a more "dynamic and connected training experience." Tiers have expanded from 10 to 12 levels to better support intermediate and advanced runners, allowing them to set higher benchmarks and challenge themselves.
The app is also adding enhanced social media sharing for milestones, personal records and route highlights, along with a new partnership with the fitness platform Strava. "Users can import their favorite Strava Routes for running, trail running, and cycling directly into Samsung Health," the company said. The new features will begin rolling out this month.

It also provides daily morning insight messages that review your previous night's sleep and offer helpful tips.
Samsung is also boosting its Running Coach app for a more "dynamic and connected training experience." Tiers have expanded from 10 to 12 levels to better support intermediate and advanced runners, allowing them to set higher benchmarks and challenge themselves.
The app is also adding enhanced social media sharing for milestones, personal records and route highlights, along with a new partnership with the fitness platform Strava. "Users can import their favorite Strava Routes for running, trail running, and cycling directly into Samsung Health," the company said. The new features will begin rolling out this month.

title_en: CMF's first portable speakers are shaped like milk cartons and pair together
title_fa: CMF's first portable speakers are shaped like milk cartons and pair together
excerpt_en: Nothing's sister company CMF announced some playful bluetooth speakers that can be paired together and even work with Auracast.
excerpt_fa: Nothing's sister company CMF announced some playful bluetooth speakers that can be paired together and even work with Auracast.
content_en:
CMF's first portable speakers are shaped like milk cartons and pair together
They look like something from Teenage Engineering or IKEA.
Surprisingly, CMF (nor its sister brand Nothing) has only now tried its hand at portable speakers. Naturally, it had to do it differently and the result is two different speaker options, both shaped like cute, vivid milk cartons.
Available now, the CMF Speaker S ($59) and Speaker M ($109) look great, with a few features and specs I'm surprised to see at this price point. Both speakers come in orange, turquoise and white, and the control knob come in different shapes and colors too; I told you: cute. You can even swap out the cover plate and knob between devices. The knob controls volume but can also skip tracks and rewind. I like the hole in the top corner of the speakers, which makes it easy to attach to a bag or tent.
The smaller Speaker S has a 45mm full-range driver, and a pair of passive radiators boost bassier tones. Meanwhile, the Speaker M has a 10W tweeter, dual drivers and even a 25W woofer, with two speaker outlets, and is roughly double the height of the Speaker S. Both speakers have Bluetooth 6.0 connectivity, IP68 dust and water resistance ratings and CMF claims both can play music for up to 18 hours. They have USB-C ports for charging, but this can also be used as audio input. The new speakers also support NFC pairing, Google Fast Pair and even Microsoft Swift Pair.
At this price, I was most surprised to see the option to pair two Speaker S or Speaker M together. Oddly, you can't combine an S and an M. They also support Auracast, which is appearing in increasingly more devices from more companies. I received a pair of the smaller speakers and they're surprisingly rich-sounding, given the size (and price). One warning: there's no USB-C cable included, but I'm sure many of us have a spare.
Like some past Teenage Engineering products, CMF says it will release the design files so devoted listeners can 3D print custom handles and accessories. Both speakers are available now on Nothing's retail site.

title_en: 8BitDo Ultimate 2C review: A fabulous Switch 2 controller at a fraction of the price
title_fa: 8BitDo Ultimate 2C review: A fabulous Switch 2 controller at a fraction of the price
excerpt_en: Hall effect sticks, haptics and extra bumpers... for how much?
excerpt_fa: Hall effect sticks, haptics and extra bumpers... for how much?
content_en:
8BitDo Ultimate 2C review: A fabulous Switch 2 controller at a fraction of the price
Hall effect sticks, haptics and extra bumpers... for how much?
The price of 8BitDo's Ultimate 2C Bluetooth Controller is bonkers in the best possible way. At just $30, the Ultimate 2C has the critical features that players expect out of a contemporary gamepad, including haptic feedback and Hall effect thumbsticks, while eschewing frivolous additions like RGB lighting and rear-grip buttons. Even then, it boasts functions that other, far more expensive Switch 2 controllers don't have. Compact, comfortable and perfectly precise, the Ultimate 2C is a fundamental gamepad that's absolutely worth every penny.
It's clear by now that 8BitDo knows how to build a great controller, and the Ultimate 2C is a pared-down paragon of this expertise, edited to showcase just the features that players really need. The Ultimate 2C has six-axis motion control, vibration, tactile bumpers and D-pad, and Hall effect triggers. There's an extra, mappable button on each shoulder, sandwiched between the main bumper and trigger, and it's particularly useful for twitch gameplay. What's more, it doesn't get in the way of the traditional shoulder array, and it can just be a little fidget toy if you don't want to map it to anything. The extra bumpers are 8BitDo's signature, at this point. The Ultimate 2C also features high-sensitivity Hall effect thumbsticks, which have a smooth glide, easy click, and lifetime no-drift guarantee.
The body of the Ultimate 2C is eggshell-style plastic, with additional texture along the grips. It's light without coming across as cheap and feels well-balanced in my hands, similar in size and shape to Nintendo's Switch 2 Pro Controller. The face buttons are shiny, pill-like domes with the letters printed on, rather than etched in. Home button aside, the small inputs in the center of the face (minus, plus, square and star) are hard to read at a glance. However, this isn't a glaring issue, as it can be solved with a little bit of time and muscle memory. The square and star buttons are flat, while the minus and plus buttons are rounded slightly, making them discernible by touch.
The Ultimate 2C can't wake up the Switch 2, though 8BitDo says it can wake the original Switch. The pricier Ultimate 2 was in the same boat until a firmware update, so perhaps this ability will come in the future (my fingers are firmly crossed).
I've yet to run into an issue with the battery life of the Ultimate 2C, since it has a 15-hour lifespan and is easy to keep charged through a standard USB-C port, with a two-hour charging time. There are three colorways available to purchase directly through 8BitDo — baby blue, pink and dark blue with a tan back — and a transparent black model exclusive to Best Buy. And yes, they really are only $30 apiece. In a world where Nintendo is charging $90 for the Switch 2 Pro Controller and comparable third-party gamepads cost around $60, this is an astounding deal.
Of course, at a third of the price of Nintendo's Switch 2 Pro Controller and half the cost of 8BitDo's Ultimate 2, the Ultimate 2C doesn't have all of the bells and whistles that it possibly could. The Ultimate 2 Bluetooth Controller is my personal favorite Switch 2 gamepad, and it has two rings of RGB lighting, buttons on the rear grips, TMR thumbsticks, Hall effect triggers with mode switching, a charging stand, 2.4G dongle, Windows compatibility, console-wake ability, and a suite of customization options through 8BitDo's Ultimate Software V2. It costs $70. Meanwhile, the fantastic and even-more-expensive Nintendo Switch 2 Pro Controller has an NFC touchpoint and an audio jack, plus proprietary soft-hit joysticks that feel like clouds. Find more details about the differences among all of these gamepads in our guide for affordable Switch 2 Pro Controller alternatives, if you're interested.
But you know what they say: Comparison is the thief of joy. The Ultimate 2C offers everything a great gamepad needs and nothing more, and it disappears into your hands once the games begin, a true sign of excellent design. It's cheap enough that you can step back and let kids abuse it, but it's also responsive, ergonomic and satisfying enough for full-time play at any age, across any genre.
Besides, it's in a league of its own when it comes to cost. You can pick up two Ultimate 2Cs for the price of one Ultimate 2 controller, and still have $10 left to invest in a fabulous co-op game like Reanimal or Overcooked 2. Or, grab three Ultimate 2Cs for the price of one Switch 2 Pro, and have yourself a little (Mario) party. The Ultimate 2C is a fully capable, comfy and cute gamepad that promises to play with precision for years to come, and it's made by a company with a fantastic reputation in the gaming accessory space. Don't question how such a spectacular Switch 2 controller costs only $30; just be glad that it does.

title_en: Beat the iPhone Duo pre-order rush with Apple's Get Ready tool
title_fa: Beat the iPhone Duo pre-order rush with Apple's Get Ready tool
excerpt_en: You can already set up your pre-order now, before the pre-orders open on Friday (October 16).
excerpt_fa: You can already set up your pre-order now, before the pre-orders open on Friday (October 16).
content_en:
Beat the iPhone Duo pre-order rush with Apple’s Get Ready tool
It's basically a pre-order opportunity before the pre-order window opens.
Apple announced the iPhone Duo last month, but it won't hit stores until October 23. However, pre-orders for the highly anticipated foldable iPhone begin this week on October 16. And if you really can't wait, here's some good news: you can already get a head start on your pre-order on Apple's website. Not only that, but carriers and retailers are already advertising their special offers for the iPhone Duo — which will probably be helpful since it isn't exactly cheap. So here's how to secure your iPhone Duo with as little hassle as possible.
Securing your iPhone Duo for launch day
If you're planning to buy the iPhone Duo directly from Apple, the company has launched a tool called Get Ready, which is the best way to speed things up. Starting today (October 12), you can already choose which model you want. Go to the Apple Online Store or use the Apple Store app and look for the iPhone Duo. Choose a color (Star White or Night Sky) and storage capacity (from 256GB to 2TB). Then, choose your carrier, decide whether or not you want to trade in your old phone and maybe add a few accessories to your purchase as well — you'll probably want to protect your new $2,000 phone with a case. AppleCare+ is also a good deal, and you can sign up for it from the purchase screen.
When all that's set, Get Ready saves you some pre-order anxiety by letting you set up a payment method and your shipping address now, before the purchase window opens on Friday. As soon as it does, Apple will place your order and ensure that you receive your new iPhone in time for launch day. Waiting until Friday to pre-order your iPhone could end up delaying shipping if you aren't quick enough, since there's usually strong demand for new products. Also, rumors suggest that there won't be many iPhone Duo units available at launch. If you use Apple's Get Ready, your chances of receiving the iPhone Duo on October 23 increase considerably.
Where to buy the iPhone Duo
Once again, you can buy your iPhone Duo directly from Apple — it's usually the easiest option, especially if you don't want to buy it tied to a specific plan or carrier. Apple is offering up to $885 in credit when you trade in an eligible iPhone, so giving up your old iPhone might be a good way to make the Duo a little less expensive. The full price starts at $1,999 for the 256GB model and can go as high as $3,199 for the 2TB model.
You can also split payments over up to 24 months, so buying the 256GB model would cost you $83.29 per month. If you sign up for the new Apple Upgrade program, the cost drops to $57.99 per month. Just now that after two years, you'll have to hand your iPhone back to Apple, pay the remaining balance to keep it or upgrade to a new device and keep paying.
Carriers are also already announcing their deals for the iPhone Duo. AT&T, for example, offers up to $1,200 in eligible trade-ins, and if you order online, you'll also earn an extra $200 per line on your plan. Best Buy will also have special deals for the iPhone Duo launch, with prices starting at $55.96 per month on an installment plan with AT&T. It's worth comparing each of these offers side by side to see which one works best for you.

title_en: Justice Department says North Koreans have infiltrated dozens of U.S. companies
title_fa: Justice Department says North Koreans have infiltrated dozens of U.S. companies
excerpt_en: U.S. authorities warn that sanctioned hackers are increasingly targeting Americans to act as facilitators between breached U.S. companies and Pyongyang.
excerpt_fa: U.S. authorities warn that sanctioned hackers are increasingly targeting Americans to act as facilitators between breached U.S. companies and Pyongyang.
content_en:
The U.S. Department of Justice is warning that hackers working for the North Korean regime are increasingly relying on Americans to facilitate the hacking of U.S. companies.
In an announcement on Tuesday, prosecutors said they have indicted and arrested at least two people, and conducted searches across dozens of suspected “laptop farms” in Texas. The computers were allegedly used by North Koreans to remotely hack into American companies and steal sensitive data.
According to the DOJ, federal authorities seized over 180 computers that they believe American companies had shipped out to their newly hired employees, not realizing that they were sanctioned North Korean spies who had used stolen identities of U.S. citizens to gain employment. The DOJ said that it raided over 40 laptop farms across Texas, the largest disclosed number of homes and residences used for facilitating North Korean hacks, which were owned by at least two American facilitators.
CrowdStrike, which helped the FBI investigate and disrupt the latest North Korean operations, said that laptop farms are “vital” to North Korea in helping its hackers overcome physical, financial, and legal challenges of not physically being in the United States.
The prosecutors said at least 70 U.S.-based companies had been infiltrated by the hackers, who are believed to have generated around $3 million in stolen funds. The DOJ did not name the affected companies, but described them as healthcare, cyber support, retail, communications, and manufacturing sectors across Ohio and 16 other states, including the District of Columbia.
“Increasingly, North Korean IT workers are turning to recruiting American facilitators to counter improved private sector detections and law enforcement actions. These workers are hiring facilitators to complete a wider variety of tasks, and in some cases subcontracting entire jobs to third-party foreign nationals,” the Justice Department said.
Oftentimes, North Korean hackers use real-looking email addresses, spoofed LinkedIn profiles, and extensive online and social media accounts as cover for their activities.
In a separate public service announcement, the FBI said that there are “thousands” of North Korean-state controlled IT workers working at Western companies, which “pose a significant national security and intellectual property theft insider threat.”
This is the latest wave of arrests, indictments, and enforcement action targeting North Korean activities in the United States in recent years. The breakaway regime has used this “remote IT workers” scheme to allow North Koreans to gain employment with U.S. and European companies, earn a wage, and then steal sensitive information and intellectual property while as employees. The victim companies are then extorted into paying the hackers further.
The remote IT workers’ scheme is one of several strands of illicit revenue that the North Korean regime aims to generate, including hacking crypto exchanges and open-source developer projects, with the aim of funding its internationally sanctioned nuclear weapons program. The regime is thought to have stolen at least $2 billion in crypto during 2025 alone.
Experts on North Korea have put the number of hacked companies and the amount of stolen crypto as likely much higher than reported.
Earlier this year, CrowdStrike said in a separate report that North Korean hackers were behind around half of all documented “hands-on-keyboard” intrusions over the past year, referring to hacks that are carried out by humans and not automated tools or AI.

title_en: Which smart TV brands offer the longest software support?
title_fa: Which smart TV brands offer the longest software support?
excerpt_en: When you spend a lot on on a TV, you expect it to last a while. But that support period varies wildly by manufacturer.
excerpt_fa: When you spend a lot on on a TV, you expect it to last a while. But that support period varies wildly by manufacturer.
content_en:
Which smart TV brands offer the longest software support?
Not all smart TVs will receive updates for long, and some don't have any specific policy.
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
No matter the price of a TV you buy, you likely consider it as a long-term investment. You thus expect it to receive support from the manufacturer for as long as possible.
In olden times, when you bought a TV, the only worry you had was it eventually breaking. But with smart TVs, there's also software to consider. Most modern TVs come with their own operating systems and apps, and need to be updated semi-regularly for the best performance and to patch security issues.
Unfortunately, there's no universal standard for how long you can expect a TV to get support for. It varies significantly by manufacturer, and the relevant information isn't always easy to find. But you're in luck, as we've done the tedious work of finding out.
Samsung offers long-term software support, but not every brand matches that commitment
If you have a Samsung TV from 2024 or later, Samsung will provide seven years of software updates for its Linux-based Tizen OS. This commitment, made in 2024, also applies to select models from 2023. That means if you have a Samsung TV from 2024, you can expect apps to work smoothly and firmware updates to roll out until at least 2031. Older models won't get major new versions of Tizen. They'll likely receive occasional maintenance or security firmware updates, though.
In early 2024, LG introduced the webOS Re:New program, which guarantees four years of webOS updates for TV models from 2022 onwards. These come with a one-year delay compared to the latest webOS release on the newest TV models. For example, webOS 26 debuted with 2026's TVs, and will come to a 2025 TV one year later.
Sony doesn't offer a fixed period of support for its TVs. Rather, it differs depending on which model you own. For example, for 2025's Sony Bravia K-65XR80M2 OLED, Sony's support page has April 2029 as the end-of-life date. Meanwhile, the Sony Bravia 2 II K-65S25VM2, which was also part of the 2025 lineup, will apparently receive security updates until June 2030.
Unlike LG and Samsung, Sony doesn't have use a proprietary TV operating system. Models released after 2021 use the Google TV platform; prior to that it was Android TV.
Like Sony, TCL doesn't guarantee a fixed period of support. All we really have to go on is the company's Software Security page, where it claims to "typically" provide security updates for at least two years after "the first shipment of a certain device model." This page doesn't explicitly mention TVs, though. Depending on the model, TCL sets primarily run on Google TV (or Android TV for older models) or Roku TV.
Software support also varies by region
In Europe, the majority of Hisense TVs run on the company's proprietary VIDAA OS. Since 2025, it has pledged support for "up to" a whopping eight years on these models. Unfortunately for those in the US, you're less likely to pick up a Hisense TV that uses VIDAA, with many models instead running Android TV, Fire TV, Google TV or Roku TV. Therefore, long-term support is in the hands of the company whose OS your TV ships with.
For a long time, Roku was known for its streaming devices and operating system that it licenses to TV brands like those listed above. But what if you buy one of Roku's own Pro, Plus or Select Series TVs? Roku doesn't specify a fixed period of support for these, and the first came out in 2023, so it's still too early to establish a pattern. But given that software is the company's focus and it frequently pushes out updates, you can reasonably expect a healthy lifespan for its TVs. Roku doesn't publish end-of-life dates for its streaming boxes either, though some people claim to have used one unit for as long as 10 years.
What about the ultra-affordable TV brands like Vizio and Insignia? The former runs its own Vizio OS, which functions in much the same way as its better-known rivals and includes more than 300 apps. No matter the price of a TV you buy, you likely consider it as a long-term investment. You thus expect it to receive support from the manufacturer for as long as possible.
In olden times, when you bought a TV, the only worry you had was it eventually breaking. But with smart TVs, there's also software to consider. Most modern TVs come with their own operating systems and apps, and need to be updated semi-regularly for the best performance and to patch security issues.
Unfortunately, there's no universal standard for how long you can expect a TV to get support for. It varies significantly by manufacturer, and the relevant information isn't always easy to find. But you're in luck, as we've done the tedious work of finding out.

That means if you have a Samsung TV from 2024, you can expect apps to work smoothly and firmware updates to roll out until at least 2031. Older models won't get major new versions of Tizen. They'll likely receive occasional maintenance or security firmware updates, though.

Unlike LG and Samsung, Sony doesn't have use a proprietary TV operating system. Models released after 2021 use the Google TV platform; prior to that it was Android TV.

title_en: Is Mini DisplayPort becoming obsolete?
title_fa: Is Mini DisplayPort becoming obsolete?
excerpt_en: Mini DisplayPort was on lots of computers for a time, but it's not nearly as common now thanks to more modern standards.
excerpt_fa: Mini DisplayPort was on lots of computers for a time, but it's not nearly as common now thanks to more modern standards.
content_en:
Is Mini DisplayPort becoming obsolete?
How Thunderbolt and USB-C replaced the need for a dedicated video port.
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
For a while, Mini DisplayPort was one of the main options for video output on smaller devices. Apple announced it in 2008 to replace interfaces like VGA and DVI with a single, slimmer connector. While it was seen on most Mac models for several years, it's since become difficult to find computers with Mini DisplayPort — even Apple has removed the port from Macs.
But does that mean it's obsolete? Not exactly, although you won't see it as often as you used to. The DisplayPort standard remains popular, especially among workstations and gaming monitors, so it's not as if the technology itself has become obsolete. But we now have another small port that's favored.
Why Mini DisplayPort faded out
Mini DisplayPort is called "mini" for a reason. The full-size version (simply called DisplayPort) supports the same core specifications, but with a larger connector. Apple always opted for the tiny version because it fits better on smaller computers like MacBooks and the Mac mini.
It doesn't matter whether you use DisplayPort (DP) or Mini DisplayPort — both can transmit video and audio through a single cable. Compared to older connectors like DVI and VGA, one of the main advantages of DisplayPort is that it offers much higher bandwidth. Depending on the generation, DP can handle resolutions up to 8K and beyond, at high frame rates (144+Hz) depending on the resolution. Meanwhile, older connectors struggle with anything above 1080p.
When the Thunderbolt standard emerged, its first two iterations used the Mini DisplayPort connector. While a standard Mini DP port only carries video and audio, Thunderbolt also supports high-speed data transfers. That meant the same connector could be used for video, audio and data — perfect for accessories like Apple's Cinema Display.
In late 2015 and 2016, the Thunderbolt 3 standard arrived and switched to the USB-C connector. Apple and other PC manufacturers quickly moved to USB-C or HDMI, leaving the Mini DisplayPort connector behind. These days, USB-C has become the standard for nearly everything. Not only can it support high-speed data transfer, but it can also handle video, audio and even the Thunderbolt protocol — all in a single, small reversible connector. Not every USB-C port can handle the same tasks, but you'll see some version of it on almost every device.
To further push Mini DisplayPort down, USB-C also supports DisplayPort Alternate Mode, meaning a compatible USB-C cable and ports can carry the same DisplayPort signal through the more modern cable. PC makers have no reason to have people buy a Mini DP-to-DP cable when they can simply buy a USB-C-to-DP cable.
Where DisplayPort still makes sense
That doesn't mean DisplayPort is gone. Of course, you may still find older hardware with Mini DisplayPort, like past laptops and graphics cards. If you still have one of these, you can buy a Mini DP-to-DP cable to connect them to a modern monitor. Since the protocol is the same, they'll communicate with each other just fine. New hardware also continues to use full-sized version of DisplayPort. It's still the standard for many high-end monitors and graphics cards.
HDMI has come a long way in recent years and can now transmit video at incredibly high resolutions. Still, DisplayPort remains the gold standard for absurdly high resolutions and refresh rates, such as 4K at 240Hz. For comparison, while HDMI 2.1 offers up to 48 Gbps of bandwidth, DisplayPort 2.1 can reach 80 Gbps. This makes a difference for those looking to get the most out of the hardware they have. HDMI 2.2 offers 96 Gbps bandwidth, which may even the field a bit once compatible devices are widely available.
Of course, when using older hardware, not everything may work as expected. VR headsets, for example, can be picky about their video signal, and they don't always play nice with Mini DisplayPort when you use an adapter. The same goes for the old Apple Cinema Display — Apple makes it clear that it doesn't work through a Thunderbolt adapter. Still, it doesn't hurt to try if you have the right cables on hand.

title_en: Science Corporation implants its vision-restoring chip in its first Stargardt disease patient
title_fa: Science Corporation implants its vision-restoring chip in its first Stargardt disease patient
excerpt_en: Max Hodak, the former president and co-founder of Neuralink, detailed onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt how his company's work with PRIMA is part of its path toward a novel brain-computer interface (BCI).
excerpt_fa: Max Hodak, the former president and co-founder of Neuralink, detailed onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt how his company's work with PRIMA is part of its path toward a novel brain-computer interface (BCI).
content_en:
Science Corporation CEO Max Hodak announced that the company has implanted its vision-restoring chip, PRIMA, into its first patient with Stargardt disease, an inherited eye disease that gradually destroys central vision. Hodak, the former president and co-founder of Neuralink, the brain implant company, explained onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt how the company’s work with PRIMA fits into its broader pursuit of a novel brain-computer interface (BCI).
“The retina is part of the central nervous system,” Hodak said. “We consider cochlear implants, retinal prostheses, motor prostheses, these are all different types of BCIs.”
Hodak outlined a vision in which BCIs expand into a wide range of medical technology applications, rather than simply being a way to control computers.
While PRIMA is commercially available in Europe for patients who’ve lost their sight to geographic atrophy, an advanced form of age-related macular degeneration, the company believes its approach can be applied to multiple diseases, including Stargardt disease, which is currently considered incurable.
Stargardt disease affects the outer retina, causing the gradual death of the eye’s light-sensing cells while potentially sparing the inner retina, the part that passes visual signals onto the brain. It causes a central blind spot that gradually enlarges over time. Approximately 150,000 people worldwide have lost vision due to the disease.
“One of the nice things about this device approach, when I was saying the brain’s a computer, vision is electrical potential, like electrical activity down the optic nerve,” Hodak said. “That’s all vision is to the brain, and so if you can get the optic nerve to signal the rest of the brain correctly, then you can provide vision to it.”
The company says its first patient with Stargardt disease received the PRIMA implant in May as part of its ongoing trial at the Sydney Eye Hospital in Australia. During the patient’s first rehabilitation session, he saw a letter, and during the second, he was able to read a word.
To use the device, patients undergo an hourlong procedure that plants a small chip in the back of their eye, where the photoreceptors have degenerated. Then they wear camera-equipped glasses that transmit a view of the world to the chip. The implant essentially works like artificial photoreceptors.
“The device that this patient has is a two millimeter by two millimeter implant placed in the back of the eye, and so it’s like looking through a straw,” Hodak said. “It is not a big field of view color vision. It’s a patch in their central vision where … it’s black and white, but it is sharp. It’s high-contrast sharp, and so they can see a couple letters at a time. The next step is to make the field of view bigger. So to make a bigger implant, you have to deal with the curvature of the eye, and we need to make the electrodes smaller so that we get closer to native levels of detail.”
He continued, “I think we have a clear path. There’s a ‘next generation’ that’s being worked on that’ll be in humans in the next year, and over the next five years, I think we’ll be able to get pretty close to native acuity.”
When Hodak founded Science Corporation in 2021 after leaving Neuralink, the company outlined plans to develop advanced neural engineering and brain-computer interface technology. But first, the company wants to prove its methods work and develop a sustainable business, which is why it’s working to restore vision with the visually impaired.
As for Science Corporation’s brain-computer interface technology, it has previously said that its sensor will be implanted inside the skull and rest on top of the brain, unlike a Neuralink device, which is inserted directly into brain tissue.
The company has said it believes the device could help address neurological conditions, such as possibly monitoring neurological activity in patients with brain tumors.
“In the near term, we’re going to be applying our first clinical indication, which hasn’t been announced publicly, is a neurodegenerative disease that everybody’s heard of,” Hodak said. “We’re also looking at stroke. For example, if you’ve lost part of your brain because it’s been dead due to stroke, if you can get connections into the deep brain in two different areas, you can imagine adding new cortical areas, just like adding new brain areas entirely — something simply not possible with conventional electrodes. But, I’d say longer term, the long-term mission of the company is to understand how the brain creates the mind and to learn to build engineered brains.”
Hodak went on to note that Science Corporation’s belief is that many people will eventually use some kind of BCI. While the company isn’t designing for “healthy 40-year-olds,” he said, it believes people will eventually need some kind of BCI by the age of 60 or 70.
“We want to figure out how do we extend not just lifespan but health span,” Hodak said.

title_en: Cerebras CEO says we’re nearing a future where everyone has a personal AI assistant at home
title_fa: Cerebras CEO says we’re nearing a future where everyone has a personal AI assistant at home
excerpt_en: Cerebras CEO Andrew Feldman predicts a future where personal AI assistants become as commonplace as household appliances, running partly on local devices and partly in the cloud.
excerpt_fa: Cerebras CEO Andrew Feldman predicts a future where personal AI assistants become as commonplace as household appliances, running partly on local devices and partly in the cloud.
content_en:
Cerebras Systems CEO and co-founder Andrew Feldman believes we’re nearing a future where everyone will have an AI appliance in their own home.
Speaking on stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 on Tuesday, the chipmaker executive answered a question about what would need to happen for AI to become a home appliance, saying, “Actually, I don’t think that’s very far away.”
He pointed to the advances in consumer AI agents, like Meta’s Muse and Instinct, the startup now valued at $10 billion, as examples of how AI is finding its footing with everyday users.
As for home AI? He predicts that we’ll have personal AI assistants that run locally.
“Just like your cell phone, they’ll do some work on device and some work going back to the cloud,” Feldman explained. “But I think they will get to know you very well, and you will have a security perimeter around them. And they will certainly have access to credit cards and be able to buy things for you,” he continued. “I think they will make a meaningful impact in making our lives better.”
Of course, for an AI chipmaker, the vision of a home AI appliance, or at least widespread consumer adoption of agentic technology, is certainly appealing.
But Feldman isn’t just working on the hardware infrastructure; he’s a personal AI user himself, saying that he now uses “a collection of agents” to sweep his calendar, pull up information about the people he’s going to have a call with, and more. While AI is already doing many of the things we used to do manually, Feldman is most excited about the new possibilities — things that weren’t possible before.
He’s leaving it up to other founders to figure out what those might be, though.
“One of the reasons I love being in infrastructure is because I don’t need the consumer-facing idea … I like building the platforms that other people’s ideas take flight on,” he said.

title_en: Industrial Next wants factory robots to switch tasks in minutes, not weeks
title_fa: Industrial Next wants factory robots to switch tasks in minutes, not weeks
excerpt_en: Industrial Next helps manufacturers automate complex, delicate tasks that have traditionally required human labor.
excerpt_fa: Industrial Next helps manufacturers automate complex, delicate tasks that have traditionally required human labor.
content_en:
In most factories, automation is fixed: robots and machines are programmed for one specific task and product. Changing a line means reprogramming and physical retooling, or swapping out equipment, which can take weeks or months. San Francisco-based Industrial Next says it’s changing that.
The startup, which presented today on the Startup Battlefield stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, builds AI-driven, self-contained robotic stations powered by proprietary foundation models that connect vision, task context and motion. The company says this lets a production line be retooled in minutes rather than weeks without traditional programming. The goal is to let manufacturers automate complex and delicate tasks that traditionally require human labor.
The company announced on stage that it’s partnering with BMW Group Technology Office to evaluate Industrial Next’s AI-powered dexterous manipulation for manufacturing.
Industrial Next was founded in 2021 by Lukas Pankau and Allen Pan, both of whom previously worked at Tesla. Pankau served as a lead electrical architect at Tesla before moving on to Waymo. Pan led Tesla’s autonomous factory efforts and later became a chief architect at autonomous driving company Neolix.
The pair came up with the idea for Industrial Next while working together at Tesla. Pankau’s first encounter with Pan was literally tripping over him as Pan was asleep on a factory catwalk after pulling an all-nighter. Although the two didn’t get along at first, they soon realized they shared an obsession with getting things done and had complementary skills.
After years of watching cutting-edge vehicle and self-driving technology get held back by decades-old factory equipment, the founders realized that manufacturing needed to be rebuilt.
“We had all these fancy things that we could do on cars. I could run machine learning algorithms to design a car for me. But I couldn’t figure out how to program a robot, and this was pretty common for engineers at Tesla,” Pankau said. “You had this massive divide, right? You had people who are really good at what they’re doing–designing cars and designing self-driving systems–and then you had them effectively stumped at the factory looking at this equipment from the 1980s. And so we started rethinking what this should look like using the technology that we have today and using everything that we know today.”
The two kept thinking about their frustrations with industrial equipment even after moving on to their next jobs. They stayed in touch, often reminiscing about the machines that never functioned the way they wanted, and eventually decided they could do better.
“I was at Waymo at the time, kind of bored out of my mind because I was missing that pace of Tesla,” Pankau said. Pan, he added, was in a similar position at Momenta, a developer of self-driving systems in China. Pan recalled their conclusion: “We’re like, we’re not getting any younger, and we’re still obviously passionate about it. We still keep complaining about industrial technology. Like, this is three years later, we should start the company.”
Pankau notes that traditional industrial robots are typically programmed to perform highly specific, repeatable tasks. As a result, even a small change in the process or product can cause the robot to fail or trigger costly downtime, which forces manufacturers to simplify their products for repeatability.
Making robots truly flexible presents a different challenge. They need enormous amounts of training data and, unlike AI models trained on the internet, robotics lacks the vast datasets needed to teach machines how to perform complex physical tasks.
“We can make robots do all these cool things like dance around, because there’s data for that, but we can’t make them assemble high-precision things,” Pankau explained. “This is where we’ve made a lot of progress on using simulated environments to do these high-precision and high-dexterity tasks. The secret sauce for the robots that we have is that we have given them an understanding of the process in general, but we build that understanding using an extremely high-fidelity simulation engine that is close to the real dynamics to where we can let the robot do these kinds of high precision tasks almost without seeing the parts at all.”
In other words, the robots practice in a highly detailed virtual world that closely mimics real-world physics. Industrial Next’s robotic stations can be reconfigured, combined, and redeployed across product lines. New tasks are taught through simulation and demonstration, rather than hard-coded scripts.
Pankau explained that some of the startup’s workstations are already used in making one of the world’s most popular smartphones. They handle tasks that manufacturers had tried and failed to automate for years, such as threading a delicate flex cable and snapping a tiny connector cap into place. (He wasn’t at liberty to disclose the customer.) He also described a “film peeling” station, where their AI-powered robots strip protective film off camera modules and buttons at or above human speed with 100% accuracy, even when moved to a new phone model and production line they have never seen.
“We started this company because that is the kind of performance that we wish we had at Tesla, where we were bypassing robot stations because we couldn’t program them effectively enough using traditional technologies,” Pankau said. “Now we want to take this to more complicated tasks than just building a phone. We ultimately want to take this to building a full car end-to-end without any human touching ever.”
To check out more of the Startup Battlefield — along with a slate of established founders and VCs whose takes on the industry you won’t want to miss — join us at Disrupt, happening this week in downtown San Francisco.

The startup, which presented today on the Startup Battlefield stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, builds AI-driven, self-contained robotic stations powered by proprietary foundation models that connect vision, task context and motion. The company says this lets a production line be retooled in minutes rather than weeks without traditional programming. The goal is to let manufacturers automate complex and delicate tasks that traditionally require human labor.
The company announced on stage that it’s partnering with BMW Group Technology Office to evaluate Industrial Next’s AI-powered dexterous manipulation for manufacturing.
Industrial Next was founded in 2021 by Lukas Pankau and Allen Pan, both of whom previously worked at Tesla. Pankau served as a lead electrical architect at Tesla before moving on to Waymo. Pan led Tesla’s autonomous factory efforts and later became a chief architect at autonomous driving company Neolix.
The pair came up with the idea for Industrial Next while working together at Tesla. Pankau’s first encounter with Pan was literally tripping over him as Pan was asleep on a factory catwalk after pulling an all-nighter. Although the two didn’t get along at first, they soon realized they shared an obsession with getting things done and had complementary skills.
After years of watching cutting-edge vehicle and self-driving technology get held back by decades-old factory equipment, the founders realized that manufacturing needed to be rebuilt.
“We had all these fancy things that we could do on cars. I could run machine learning algorithms to design a car for me. But I couldn’t figure out how to program a robot, and this was pretty common for engineers at Tesla,” Pankau said. “You had this massive divide, right? You had people who are really good at what they’re doing–designing cars and designing self-driving systems–and then you had them effectively stumped at the factory looking at this equipment from the 1980s. And so we started rethinking what this should look like using the technology that we have today and using everything that we know today.”
The two kept thinking about their frustrations with industrial equipment even after moving on to their next jobs. They stayed in touch, often reminiscing about the machines that never functioned the way they wanted, and eventually decided they could do better.
“I was at Waymo at the time, kind of bored out of my mind because I was missing that pace of Tesla,” Pankau said. Pan, he added, was in a similar position at Momenta, a developer of self-driving systems in China. Pan recalled their conclusion: “We’re like, we’re not getting any younger, and we’re still obviously passionate about it. We still keep complaining about industrial technology. Like, this is three years later, we should start the company.”
Pankau notes that traditional industrial robots are typically programmed to perform highly specific, repeatable tasks. As a result, even a small change in the process or product can cause the robot to fail or trigger costly downtime, which forces manufacturers to simplify their products for repeatability.
Making robots truly flexible presents a different challenge. They need enormous amounts of training data and, unlike AI models trained on the internet, robotics lacks the vast datasets needed to teach machines how to perform complex physical tasks.
“We can make robots do all these cool things like dance around, because there’s data for that, but we can’t make them assemble high-precision things,” Pankau explained. “This is where we’ve made a lot of progress on using simulated environments to do these high-precision and high-dexterity tasks. The secret sauce for the robots that we have is that we have given them an understanding of the process in general, but we build that understanding using an extremely high-fidelity simulation engine that is close to the real dynamics to where we can let the robot do these kinds of high precision tasks almost without seeing the parts at all.”
In other words, the robots practice in a highly detailed virtual world that closely mimics real-world physics. Industrial Next’s robotic stations can be reconfigured, combined, and redeployed across product lines. New tasks are taught through simulation and demonstration, rather than hard-coded scripts.
Pankau explained that some of the startup’s workstations are already used in making one of the world’s most popular smartphones. They handle tasks that manufacturers had tried and failed to automate for years, such as threading a delicate flex cable and snapping a tiny connector cap into place. (He wasn’t at liberty to disclose the customer.) He also described a “film peeling” station, where their AI-powered robots strip protective film off camera modules and buttons at or above human speed with 100% accuracy, even when moved to a new phone model and production line they have never seen.
“We started this company because that is the kind of performance that we wish we had at Tesla, where we were bypassing robot stations because we couldn’t program them effectively enough using traditional technologies,” Pankau said. “Now we want to take this to more complicated tasks than just building a phone. We ultimately want to take this to building a full car end-to-end without any human touching ever.”
To check out more of the Startup Battlefield — along with a slate of established founders and VCs whose takes on the industry you won’t want to miss — join us at Disrupt, happening this week in downtown San Francisco.

title_en: How to improve your online privacy and security in Google Chrome
title_fa: How to improve your online privacy and security in Google Chrome
excerpt_en: Google has much to gain by collecting data from you through your activity on Chrome, but you can make it harder.
excerpt_fa: Google has much to gain by collecting data from you through your activity on Chrome, but you can make it harder.
content_en:
How to improve your online privacy and security in Google Chrome
Google has a vested interest in collecting and selling your data, but that doesn't mean protecting yourself is impossible.
Google Chrome is easily the biggest browser in the game — and the hottest commodity in that game is data. Whenever you surf the web, your personal data becomes a product, whether you surrender it willingly or unknowingly to any number of vendors, or a hacker slips through the cracks and makes off with your information. Fortunately, there are many ways to secure your Google account, and not just with Chrome's new fortnightly updates.
Of course, when it comes to privacy, using Chrome might be starting off on the wrong foot. While it has many upsides in terms of security, Google's privacy measures are flawed compared to a browser like Firefox; your Google account collects a great deal of day-to-day information about you, including app usage and browser history. However, if you're already set up with Google, there are some measures you can take to improve your security.
Improving your privacy settings in Google Chrome
First things first, head to the three dots in the top right of your browser, scroll down to Settings and head to Privacy and security. Right away, you'll want to tap on Third-party cookies and select Block third-party cookies, then turn on Do Not Track. The latter is only a request, so sites that receive the request when you enter them can choose to acknowledge or ignore that request at their own discretion.
Before looking at more settings in this area, there are more privacy-specific toggles to be checked elsewhere. If you click on your Google profile icon instead of the three dots and navigate to Manage your Google Account > Data & privacy, you can toggle off Web & App Activity, which is another setting Google uses to extract more of your data. Once you've done that, you can also turn off Timeline, which is the setting Google uses to track your location history, as well as Personalize Search, which collects data to tailor search results and AI responses to your activity. To further depersonalize ads (meaning more protection for your data from Google's modus operandi), you can turn off personalized ads in My Ad Center.
Tightening security in Google Chrome
Turning attention to security, whether it's Chrome's Gemini Nano scam protection or its Safety Check review system, the browser is much more robust here than with privacy. First, head back to the three-dot menu > Settings > Privacy and security, where you can click on Go to Safety Check, which will scan for any security issues you might have and tell you how to resolve them. In addition to any immediate problems, it will let you know if you're reusing any passwords too much and if you need a Chrome update. Chrome's Safety Check will also constantly run in the background, keeping you alert to threats as they arise.
While you're in the Privacy and security zone, you should take a gander at the Safe Browsing section. There are three types of Safe Browsing, with the default Standard protection standing constant vigil against potentially dangerous websites, downloads and extensions. Here, you can turn on Enhanced protection to add an AI-powered layer of security to your searching, though it's fine to forgo if you're not fond of AI-charged zealotry. Right below that, you can also turn on Always use secure connections, which will grant an advance warning if a site doesn't support secure connections.
